answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type (root account): Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (and child types such as Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and /mongodbDatabases/collections for MongoDB API resources).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core Azure CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create --name <account> --resource-group <rg> --kind MongoDB --default-consistency-level Session. The az cosmosdb group is part of the core CLI (no separate extension required for basic account operations).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for the account. MongoDB DB & collection child resources: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases and Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases/collections. Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account for the account; plus azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database and azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection to create Mongo DBs/collections.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical MongoDB URI for the Cosmos/Mongo-compatible account: mongodb://<user>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. An SRV form is also common: mongodb+srv://<user>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Important options: ssl=true (TLS), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false (recommended for Cosmos Mongo API), and appropriate auth credentials (SCRAM username/password).

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity for the Cosmos DB Mongo-compatible service is billed by provisioned throughput in Request Units (RU/s) or by serverless (when enabled). You can choose provisioned RU/s (fixed or autoscale) or serverless where available. It is not billed by vCores in the classic Cosmos DB API model.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Data-plane authentication for the MongoDB API is primarily via MongoDB credentials (SCRAM username/password created for the DB/account) included in the Mongo URI. Management operations use Azure RBAC / Microsoft Entra ID. As of my knowledge cutoff, direct Microsoft Entra ID (AAD) authentication for the MongoDB wire protocol is not generally available — drivers normally connect with SCRAM credentials. (Management-plane auth uses az login / Azure AD.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python, mongodb driver for Node.js, etc.) because the service exposes the MongoDB wire protocol. There is no separate data-plane, Mongo-specific Azure SDK required for read/write operations; Azure SDKs are for management and admin tasks.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: From my prior knowledge of Mongo-compatible vector features (and based on the sample spec), expected supported index algorithms include HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. The creation is done with a Mongo createIndex call on the vector field. Example form I would use: db.pubmed_abstracts.createIndex({embedding: 'vector'}, {name: 'emb_idx', algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536, metric: 'cosine'}) — (note: exact option names may vary by service; this is the concrete command I'd try first).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full‑text: use MongoDB text indexes ($text) for basic full-text search. For richer/full feature search or hybrid (keyword + vector) you typically either: 1) perform a vector nearest‑neighbour search then re‑rank results by text match in the application, or 2) integrate with a search service (Azure Cognitive Search) that supports hybrid ranking. There is no single built‑in hybrid operator in the standard MongoDB API I know of.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Typically the Mongo-compatible Azure service supports a specific MongoDB server/wire version (historically 3.6/4.0/4.2/4.4/5.0 and more recently newer versions as the service evolves). You should assume some newer Mongo server features may be missing (server-side JavaScript, some aggregation pipeline features, certain writeConcern behaviors, and advanced sharding/replica set admin commands). If you need a particular Mongo server version feature set, explicitly check the account's configured MongoDB feature/version. (I would start by assuming support up through 5.x unless the account advertises 6/7 support.)

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: Run a local MongoDB server for dev: docker run -p 27017:27017 --name mongo mongo:7.0 (or the server version matching the target cluster). There is an Azure Cosmos DB emulator for SQL/Table APIs, but historically it did not reliably emulate the MongoDB API; so prefer a real Mongo docker image matching the wire version. Connect locally on port 27017.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams are not reliably supported across all Mongo-compatible configurations of the Azure service. Cosmos DB has its own change feed feature (for SQL/Gremlin APIs), but MongoDB change streams support was historically limited. Treat change streams as not guaranteed; if you need change notifications use the provider's change feed or a supported service feature and verify on the target account whether change streams are enabled.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the service-specific MCP server named 'documentdb' for data‑plane inspection and operations. The general Azure MCP server handles management-plane resources but the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane tooling (inspect collections, indexes and query plans) targeted to this service.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically Microsoft used the name Azure DocumentDB for the original document database service which evolved and was rebranded to Azure Cosmos DB. The Cosmos DB service now exposes multiple APIs including a MongoDB-compatible API; the old 'DocumentDB' name is the ancestor of Cosmos. The independent open-source 'DocumentDB' project (if referenced) is separate — Microsoft’s DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is a managed platform service, not the same as any unrelated open-source project.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath the Mongo-compatible Azure offering is the provider's proprietary storage/engine (Cosmos DB's engine in Microsoft's managed offering), not a stock mongod process. That means application code should use standard MongoDB drivers and queries will mostly work, but some server-side behaviors, limits, and edge-case features (aggregation operators, transactions semantics, change streams, admin commands) can differ — so test critical behaviors against the actual service.

answers.question: What client code and connection pattern will the sample use to connect to the cluster at runtime?
answers.answer: Use the standard pymongo driver and read the URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. Example: from pymongo import MongoClient; import os; client = MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'], serverSelectionTimeoutMS=5000). Do not print or store the raw URI. Ensure tls/ssl is enabled by the URI (ssl=true) and set appropriate timeouts.

answers.question: What database and collection names will the sample create/use?
answers.answer: Use database name sample_healthcare_17. Collections: pubmed_abstracts for the documents (fields: _id, pmid, year, title, abstract, embedding) and embeddings (if you prefer a separate embeddings collection) — by default put embedding vector into pubmed_abstracts.embedding to keep citations, pmid and year together.

answers.question: What vector index definition will the sample try to create for semantic search?
answers.answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field. Concrete command I will run first: db.pubmed_abstracts.createIndex({embedding: 'vector'}, {name: 'emb_idx', algorithm: 'hnsw', dims: 1536, metric: 'cosine'}). If the server rejects option names, I'll adapt to the service's exact createIndex syntax but this is the first concrete attempt.

answers.question: What embedding dimensionality and embedding provider will the pipeline assume?
answers.answer: Assume 1536 dimensions (common for many open embeddings and fits LlamaIndex workflows). The pipeline will call the configured embedding provider in the sample (user-specified in config) and store 1536-d float arrays in the embedding field. If the actual provider returns a different size the code will validate and fail fast.

answers.question: What query pattern will the sample use to implement RAG ranking and citations?
answers.answer: Run a k-NN vector search (via the service's vector query operator, e.g. a find with a vector search operator or a special $vectorSearch stage) to get the top N semantically-similar docs, then re-rank or filter by text/citation fields in the application. Return PubMed ID (pmid) and year from each hit as the citation. Concrete first attempt: use the find/aggregation pattern with a vector search stage, e.g. db.pubmed_abstracts.find({$vectorSearch: {knn: {vector: [...], field: 'embedding', k: 10}}}) and then project pmid and year.
